title: How Rockets Reach Space
summary: How a rocket uses hot gas, thrust, stages, and great speed to escape the pull of gravity and reach orbit, and how Saudi astronauts have traveled to space.
poll: Going to space is the hardest job a machine can do.

versions.title: Up to Space
versions.text:
Blow up a balloon. Now let it go. Air rushes out the back. The balloon zooms off! A rocket works like that.

A rocket burns fuel. The fuel makes hot gas. The gas shoots out the back. It shoots out fast. It pushes the rocket up.

A rocket has to push hard. Earth pulls on it. That pull holds us down. So a rocket needs lots of fuel.

Big rockets have parts. Each part is a stage. A stage can run out of fuel. Then it drops off. Now the rocket is light. It can go fast.

The rocket must go very fast. Then it can stay up. It goes round and round the Earth. This path is an orbit.

A man or a woman who goes to space is an astronaut. In 1985, a Saudi man went to space. He was the first. In 2023, two more Saudi astronauts went up.

versions.title: Up to Space
versions.text:
Blow up a balloon. Then let it go. Air rushes out the back. The balloon zooms the other way! A rocket works the same way.

A rocket burns fuel. The fuel makes hot gas. The gas shoots out the bottom very fast. It rushes down. That pushes the rocket up.

A rocket has to push very hard. It must beat the pull of Earth. This pull holds us all down. That is why a rocket needs so much fuel.

Big rockets are built in parts. Each part is called a stage. A stage can run out of fuel. Then it drops off. The rocket is light now. It can go faster.

To stay in space, a rocket must go very fast. Then it can go around the Earth again and again. This path is called an orbit.

A person who goes to space is called an astronaut. In 1985, a Saudi prince went to space. He was the first Saudi astronaut. In 2023, two more Saudi astronauts went up.

versions.title: How Rockets Reach Space
versions.text:
Blow up a balloon and then let it go. Air rushes out of the back, and the balloon zooms off the other way! A big rocket uses the same idea.

A rocket burns fuel in its engines. The fuel makes hot gas. The gas blasts out of the bottom very fast. As the gas rushes down, it pushes the rocket up.

Lifting off is hard work. A rocket must beat gravity. Gravity is the pull that holds things down on Earth. That is why a rocket needs a huge load of fuel.

Big rockets are built in parts. Each part is called a stage. When a stage uses up its fuel, it drops away. The rocket gets lighter, so it can speed up.

To stay in space, a rocket must go very, very fast. Then it can keep falling around the Earth and never hit the ground. This path is called an orbit.

A person who goes to space is called an astronaut. In 1985, Prince Sultan bin Salman became the first Saudi astronaut. In 2023, two more Saudi astronauts flew to the space station.

versions.title: How Rockets Reach Space
versions.text:
Blow up a balloon and then let it go. Air rushes out of the back. The balloon zooms off the other way! A giant rocket uses the same idea.

A rocket burns fuel inside its engines. The burning fuel makes hot gas. The gas blasts out of the bottom of the rocket at great speed. As the gas rushes down, it pushes the rocket up.

Lifting off takes a lot of power. A rocket must beat gravity, the pull that holds everything down on Earth. That is why most of a rocket's weight at launch is fuel.

Big rockets are built in parts called stages. When a stage uses up its fuel, it drops away and falls back. The rocket gets lighter. Now it can speed up more easily.

To stay in space, a rocket must go very fast, about 28,000 kilometers an hour. At that speed, it keeps falling around the Earth but never hits the ground. This curved path is called an orbit.

A person who travels to space is called an astronaut. In 1985, Prince Sultan bin Salman became the first Saudi and first Arab astronaut. In 2023, two more Saudi astronauts, Rayyanah Barnawi and Ali AlQarni, flew to the space station.

versions.title: How Rockets Reach Space
versions.text:
Blow up a balloon and let it go, and it zooms around the room as air rushes out of the back. A rocket works on the same idea, but with far more power.

Inside a rocket's engine, fuel burns with oxygen and creates hot gas. The gas blasts out of a bell-shaped opening called a nozzle. As the gas rushes down, it pushes the rocket up. This upward push is called thrust.

Lifting off is a battle against gravity, the force that pulls everything toward Earth. A rocket can only rise when its thrust is greater than its weight. That is why most of a rocket's weight at launch is fuel.

There is no air to breathe in space, so a rocket carries its own oxygen in a tank. This lets the fuel keep burning even after the rocket leaves the air behind.

Large rockets are built in stages. When a stage runs out of fuel, it falls away, and the lighter rocket speeds up. Some modern boosters even fly back and land so they can be used again. These reusable rockets save money.

To stay in orbit, a spacecraft must travel about 28,000 kilometers an hour. At that speed, it keeps falling around Earth instead of falling down to it.

In 1985, Prince Sultan bin Salman became the first Arab astronaut. In 2023, Saudi astronauts Rayyanah Barnawi and Ali AlQarni rode a rocket to the International Space Station.

versions.text:
Blow up a balloon and release it, and it zooms around the room as air rushes out of the back. A rocket works on the same idea, but with far more power.

Inside a rocket's engine, fuel burns with oxygen and makes very hot gas. The gas blasts out of a bell-shaped opening called a nozzle. As the gas rushes down, it pushes the rocket up, and this upward push is called thrust.

Lifting off is a battle against gravity, the force that pulls everything toward Earth. A rocket can only rise when its thrust is greater than its weight. That is why most of a rocket's weight at launch is fuel.

There is no air to breathe in space, so a rocket carries its own oxygen in a separate tank. This lets the fuel keep burning even after the rocket has left the air behind.

Large rockets are built in stages. When a stage runs out of fuel, it falls away, and the lighter rocket speeds up. Some modern boosters even fly back to Earth and land standing up so they can be used again. These reusable rockets help make trips to space cost less.

To stay in orbit, a spacecraft must travel about 28,000 kilometers an hour. At that speed, it keeps falling around Earth instead of falling down to it.

In 1985, Prince Sultan bin Salman became the first Arab astronaut. In 2023, Saudi astronauts Rayyanah Barnawi and Ali AlQarni rode a rocket to the International Space Station, where they did science work for about a week.

versions.title: How Rockets Reach Space
versions.text:
If you blow up a balloon and release it, the balloon zooms wildly around the room as air rushes out of the back. A rocket operates on the same principle, although it uses vastly more power.

Inside a rocket's engine, fuel burns with oxygen and produces extremely hot gas, which blasts out of a bell-shaped opening called a nozzle. As the gas rushes downward, it pushes the rocket upward, and scientists call this upward force thrust.

Lifting off is a battle against gravity, the force that pulls everything toward Earth. A rocket can only rise when its thrust is greater than its weight, which explains why most of a rocket's weight at launch is fuel.

Because there is no air to breathe in space, a rocket carries its own supply of oxygen in a separate tank. This allows the fuel to continue burning even after the rocket has left the atmosphere behind.

Large rockets are constructed in sections called stages, rather than as one single piece. When a stage uses up its fuel, it detaches and falls away, and the lighter rocket speeds up more efficiently. Some modern boosters even fly back to Earth and land upright so that they can be launched again, and these reusable rockets help make spaceflight less expensive.

To remain in orbit, a spacecraft must travel about 28,000 kilometers an hour. At that tremendous speed, it keeps falling around Earth instead of falling down to it, and the curved path it follows is called an orbit.

In 1985, Prince Sultan bin Salman became the first Arab astronaut. In 2023, Saudi astronauts Rayyanah Barnawi and Ali AlQarni traveled aboard a rocket to the International Space Station, where they carried out scientific experiments for about a week.

versions.title: The Physics of Reaching Orbit
versions.text:
If you inflate a balloon and release it, the balloon zooms unpredictably around the room as air rushes out of the back. A rocket operates on the same principle, which the scientist Isaac Newton described in his third law of motion: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

Inside a rocket's engine, propellant burns and produces extremely hot gas. This gas blasts out of a bell-shaped nozzle. As the gas is forced downward, the rocket is pushed upward, and this upward force is called thrust. A rocket can only leave the launch pad when its thrust is greater than its weight, which is why most of its weight at liftoff is propellant.

Propellant has two parts: a fuel and an oxidizer, which supplies the oxygen that the fuel needs in order to burn. Because there is no air in space, a rocket must carry its oxidizer with it, so that its engines can keep firing after it has left the atmosphere.

Large rockets are built in stages. When a stage has used up its propellant, it separates and falls away, so that the remaining rocket is lighter and can accelerate more efficiently. Some modern boosters even fly back to Earth and land upright, which makes them reusable and helps reduce the cost of spaceflight.

Space is often said to begin about 100 kilometers above the ground, but reaching that height is not enough. To stay in orbit, a spacecraft needs a sideways velocity of about 28,000 kilometers an hour, so that it keeps falling around Earth instead of falling back down to it. Many rockets launch toward the east. Many launch sites are built near the equator, because the spinning Earth gives them extra speed.

The International Space Station, for example, circles about 400 kilometers above Earth and completes one orbit roughly every ninety minutes, which means that the astronauts on board can see about sixteen sunrises each day. They float inside the station not because gravity has disappeared, but because they and the station are falling around Earth together.

In 1985, Prince Sultan bin Salman became the first Arab astronaut, and in 2023, Saudi astronauts Rayyanah Barnawi and Ali AlQarni traveled to the International Space Station.

versions.title: The Physics of Reaching Orbit
versions.text:
If you inflate a balloon and release it, the balloon zooms unpredictably around the room as air rushes out of the back. A rocket operates on an identical principle, which the scientist Isaac Newton articulated in his third law of motion: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

Inside a rocket's engine, propellant combusts and produces extremely hot gas, which accelerates out of a bell-shaped nozzle. As the gas is forced downward, the rocket is propelled upward, and this upward force is called thrust. A rocket can only leave the launch pad when its thrust exceeds its weight, which is precisely why the overwhelming majority of its mass at liftoff consists of propellant.

Propellant has two components: a fuel and an oxidizer, which supplies the oxygen that the fuel requires for combustion. Because there is no atmospheric oxygen in space, a rocket must transport its oxidizer along with it, so that its engines can continue operating after it has departed from the atmosphere.

Large rockets are deliberately constructed in multiple separate stages, and when a stage has exhausted its propellant, it separates and falls away, so that the remaining vehicle is lighter and can accelerate more efficiently. Certain modern boosters even return to Earth and land vertically, which makes them reusable and substantially reduces the expense of spaceflight.

Space is conventionally considered to begin approximately 100 kilometers above the ground, but reaching that altitude is insufficient. To remain in orbit, a spacecraft requires a horizontal velocity of approximately 28,000 kilometers an hour, so that it continuously falls around Earth instead of descending back to the surface. Many rockets launch toward the east, and numerous launch facilities are located near the equator, because the rotating planet contributes additional velocity.

The International Space Station, for example, circles approximately 400 kilometers above Earth and completes one orbit roughly every ninety minutes, which means that the astronauts aboard can witness approximately sixteen sunrises daily. They float weightlessly inside the station not because gravity has vanished, but because both they and the station are continuously falling around the planet simultaneously.

In 1985, Prince Sultan bin Salman became the first Arab astronaut when he flew aboard the American space shuttle Discovery, and in 2023, Saudi astronauts Rayyanah Barnawi and Ali AlQarni traveled to the International Space Station.

keyWords.definition: something that is burned to make power or heat
keyWords.example: The car stopped because it ran out of fuel.

keyWords.definition: a form of matter, like air or steam, that can spread out to fill any space
keyWords.example: Steam is a gas that rises from hot tea.

keyWords.definition: one part or section of a rocket that has its own engines and fuel
keyWords.example: The first stage of the toy rocket popped off with a click.

keyWords.definition: the curved path an object takes as it goes around a planet or star
keyWords.example: The Moon takes about a month to finish one orbit around Earth.

keyWords.definition: a person who is trained to travel in space
keyWords.example: The astronaut waved to the crowd before climbing into the spacecraft.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to make a balloon
How a rocket gets up into space
Why the Moon goes around Earth
How to become a pilot
questions.why: The article explains how a rocket uses fuel, hot gas, stages, and speed to reach space.

wrong.A: The balloon is only an example to explain how rockets work.
wrong.C: The Moon is not talked about.
wrong.D: Pilots are not part of the article.

questions.stem: What does the burning fuel make?
options: Cold water
Thick smoke clouds that hold the rocket
Hot gas
Ice
questions.why: The article says the fuel makes hot gas that shoots out the back.

wrong.A: Water is not made by the fuel in the article.
wrong.B: The article does not say clouds hold the rocket up.
wrong.D: Burning fuel is hot, not icy.

questions.stem: What happens to a stage when it runs out of fuel?
options: It drops off.
It fills up again in the sky.
It turns into a balloon.
It lands on the Moon.
questions.why: The article says a stage that runs out of fuel drops off.

wrong.B: There is no way to fill it up in the sky.
wrong.C: The balloon is only an example.
wrong.D: The article does not say stages land on the Moon.

questions.stem: Why does a rocket go faster after a stage drops off?
options: The stage pushes it from below.
The air gets warmer.
Earth stops pulling on it.
The rocket is lighter.
questions.why: The article explains that after a stage drops off, the rocket is light, so it can go faster.

wrong.A: The stage falls away; it does not push.
wrong.B: Warm air is not given as a reason.
wrong.C: Earth still pulls on the rocket.

questions.stem: In the article, a balloon "zooms" across the room. What does zooms mean?
options: Moves very fast
Gets bigger
Falls asleep
Turns a new color
questions.why: Zooms means moves very fast, like the balloon pushed by the rushing air.

wrong.B: The balloon gets smaller as air rushes out, not bigger.
wrong.D: Nothing in the article says the balloon changes color.

questions.stem: Why does the author start with a balloon?
options: To show a fun party game
To tell how balloons are made
To compare a balloon to the Moon in the night sky
To help readers picture how a rocket works
questions.why: The balloon is a simple example most readers know, so it helps them understand how gas pushing out makes a rocket move.

wrong.A: The balloon is not part of a game in the article.
wrong.B: The article never explains how balloons are made.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if a rocket did not have enough fuel?
options: It would go faster.
It would turn into an orbit.
It could not get up into space.
It would get more stages.
questions.why: The article says a rocket needs lots of fuel to push hard against Earth's pull, so with too little fuel it could not reach space.

wrong.A: Less fuel means less push, not more speed.
wrong.B: An orbit is a path, not something a rocket turns into.
wrong.D: Running low on fuel does not add stages.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Saudi Arabia from the end of the article?
options: It has never sent any of its people to space.
Its people have traveled to space more than once.
It built the first rocket.
Its astronauts live on the Moon.
questions.why: The article says a Saudi astronaut went in 1985 and two more went in 2023, so Saudis have gone to space more than once.

wrong.A: The article names Saudi astronauts who went to space.
wrong.C: The article does not say who built the first rocket.
wrong.D: No one in the article lives on the Moon.

LOW.prompt: Use the balloon example to explain how a rocket moves up. Write three or four sentences.
checklist: I explained that gas rushes out one way and pushes the rocket the other way.
I used the words fuel and gas.
I wrote my ideas in the right order.

keyWords.definition: a strong push that moves something forward or upward
keyWords.example: The jet engines gave the plane enough thrust to take off.

keyWords.definition: a gas in the air that people breathe and that fire needs to burn
keyWords.example: A candle goes out when you cover it, because it runs out of oxygen.

keyWords.definition: a narrow opening at the end of a pipe or engine that directs a flow of liquid or gas
keyWords.example: He twisted the nozzle on the hose to make a fine spray.

keyWords.definition: the force that pulls objects toward each other, like the pull of Earth
keyWords.example: Gravity makes a ball fall back down after you throw it.
We carry reusable bags to the market instead of plastic ones.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea?
options: Rockets reach space by making enough thrust to beat gravity and then going fast enough to stay in orbit.
Rockets are too expensive to build.
Balloons and rockets are the same size.
Only Saudi astronauts can visit the space station.
questions.why: The article explains thrust, carrying oxygen, stages, and orbital speed, which together let a rocket reach and stay in space.

wrong.B: The article says reusable rockets lower costs; cost is not the main idea.
wrong.C: Balloons are only a comparison for how rockets move.
wrong.D: The article does not say only Saudis visit the station.

questions.stem: When can a rocket rise off the launch pad?
options: When the nozzle is closed
When its thrust is greater than its weight
When the air around the launch pad is very cold
When it reaches orbit
questions.why: The article says a rocket can only rise when its thrust is greater than its weight.

wrong.A: A closed nozzle would block the gas, not lift the rocket.
wrong.C: Air temperature is not given as a reason.
wrong.D: A rocket must rise first before it can reach orbit.

questions.stem: Why does a rocket carry its own oxygen?
options: So astronauts can open the windows
To make the rocket heavier so it stays steady and does not tip over
Because there is no air in space to help the fuel burn
To cool down the engines
questions.why: The article explains there is no air in space, so the rocket brings oxygen to keep the fuel burning.

wrong.A: Rockets do not open windows in space.
wrong.B: Extra weight is a problem for rockets, not a goal.
wrong.D: Oxygen helps fuel burn; the article does not say it cools engines.

questions.stem: In the article, the gas blasts out of a "nozzle." What is a nozzle?
options: A large fuel tank on the side of the rocket
A seat for the astronaut
A window at the top of the rocket
A shaped opening that the gas shoots out of
questions.why: The article describes the nozzle as a bell-shaped opening that the hot gas blasts out of.

wrong.A: Fuel tanks hold fuel; the nozzle lets gas out.
wrong.C: The nozzle is at the bottom, where the gas leaves.

questions.stem: Put these events in order: (1) a stage falls away, (2) fuel burns and gas blasts out, (3) the lighter rocket speeds up.
questions.why: First fuel burns to lift the rocket, then an empty stage falls away, and then the lighter rocket speeds up.

wrong.A: A stage cannot fall away before fuel has burned.
wrong.B: The rocket speeds up after the stage drops, not first.
wrong.D: The speed-up comes after the stage falls away.

questions.stem: Why are reusable boosters important?
options: They make trips to space cost less.
They let rockets fly without fuel.
They make the rocket heavier.
They carry the astronauts home.
questions.why: Boosters that land can be launched again, so builders do not need a new one for every trip, which saves money.

wrong.C: Boosters fall away to make the rocket lighter.
wrong.D: The article says boosters land; it does not say they carry astronauts.

questions.stem: A spacecraft in orbit is described as "falling around Earth." What does this suggest?
options: It is about to crash.
Its engines have stopped working.
It is so far away that gravity can no longer pull on it at all.
It moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing the ground.
questions.why: At about 28,000 kilometers an hour, the craft keeps falling, but its speed carries it around Earth instead of down to it.

wrong.A: It falls around Earth, not down to it.
wrong.B: The article does not say its engines stopped.
wrong.C: Gravity still pulls on it; that is why it falls.

questions.stem: How does the author organize most of the article?
options: By telling a story about one astronaut's life from childhood to space
By explaining each step a rocket needs to reach space
By listing rockets from smallest to largest
By comparing rockets with airplanes
questions.why: The article moves through the steps: making thrust, beating gravity, carrying oxygen, dropping stages, and reaching orbital speed.

wrong.A: Astronauts are only mentioned at the end.
wrong.C: Rockets are not listed by size.

checklist: I named two problems, such as gravity or no air in space.
I explained how the rocket solves each problem.
I used at least two key words correctly.

keyWords.definition: the fuel and other material burned in a rocket engine to push it forward
keyWords.example: Engineers loaded the propellant into the rocket hours before launch.

keyWords.definition: a substance that supplies oxygen so that a fuel can burn
keyWords.example: Without an oxidizer, the fuel in the test engine would not light.

keyWords.definition: the speed of something in a particular direction
keyWords.example: The ball left the bat with such velocity that it flew over the fence.

keyWords.definition: the layer of air that surrounds a planet
keyWords.example: Clouds and weather form in the lowest part of Earth's atmosphere.

keyWords.definition: the imaginary line around the middle of Earth, halfway between the North and South Poles

questions.stem: What is the central idea of the article?
options: Rockets are dangerous and should be replaced by airplanes.
Reaching orbit depends on Newton's third law, carrying an oxidizer, shedding stages, and gaining enough sideways speed.
Newton invented the first rocket.
Space begins exactly 100 kilometers above the ground.
questions.why: The article connects these scientific ideas to explain how a rocket gets to orbit and stays there.

wrong.A: The article never compares rockets with airplanes.
wrong.C: Newton described a law of motion; the article does not say he built a rocket.
wrong.D: This is one detail, and the article says reaching that height is not enough.

questions.stem: According to the article, what does Newton's third law state?
options: Heavy objects always fall faster than light ones, even in space.
Objects in space have no weight.
For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
Fuel always needs air to burn.
questions.why: The article quotes the third law as: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

wrong.A: This is not stated in the article.
wrong.B: The article says astronauts float because they are falling, not because they have no weight.
wrong.D: This is not a law of motion, and rockets carry an oxidizer instead.

questions.stem: What are the two parts of propellant?
options: Air and water
A fuel and an oxidizer
A nozzle and a fuel tank
Thrust and gravity together
questions.why: The article says propellant has two components: a fuel and an oxidizer.

wrong.A: Rockets do not use air from outside in space.
wrong.C: These are rocket parts, not parts of propellant.

questions.stem: Why do many launch sites sit near the equator?
options: The air there contains more oxygen.
Gravity is turned off near the equator.
Rockets can avoid bad weather there.
Earth's rotation gives rockets extra speed there.
questions.why: The article says the rotating Earth provides additional speed, which helps rockets launched toward the east.

wrong.A: Oxygen in the air is not the reason given.
wrong.C: Weather is not mentioned as a reason.

questions.stem: The article says astronauts "float" in the space station. Based on the article, what is the best explanation?
options: They and the station are falling around Earth together.
There is no gravity at all once you are 400 kilometers above Earth.
The station is filled with a special light gas.
The astronauts wear devices that lift them.
questions.why: The article states that astronauts float because they and the station are continuously falling around Earth together, not because gravity is gone.

wrong.B: The article says gravity has not disappeared.

questions.stem: In the article, a stage has "exhausted" its propellant. What does exhausted mean here?
options: Very tired after hard work
Heated up
Used up completely
Mixed with oxygen
questions.why: When a stage has exhausted its propellant, it has used all of it, so it separates and falls away.

wrong.A: This is another meaning of exhausted, but a rocket stage cannot feel tired.
wrong.B: Heating is not what happens when the propellant runs out.
wrong.D: Mixing with oxygen is how propellant burns, not what exhausted means.

questions.stem: How is a rocket in space different from a fire on Earth?
options: A rocket must bring its own oxidizer, while a fire on Earth uses oxygen from the air.
A fire on Earth needs no fuel at all.
A rocket uses no fuel in space.
A fire on Earth burns better in a vacuum.
questions.why: The article explains that there is no air in space, so the rocket must carry its oxidizer, unlike a fire that takes oxygen from the surrounding air.
